📍 Startup India, DPIIT at AIC-SMUTBI, Sikkim

Shri Ateesh Kumar Singh, Additional Secretary, DPIIT, graced the North-East Entrepreneurs' Meet 2026 at AIC-SMUTBI, Sikkim Manipal University, as Chief Guest on 27 September 2026.

In his address, Shri Ateesh Kumar Singh celebrated the immense entrepreneurial potential of the Northeast, urging the region to embrace and build on its own distinctive strengths, such as organic agriculture, tourism, wellness, and natural resources, to create globally competitive businesses rooted in local identity. He highlighted the evolving DPIIT policy framework, including expanded recognition norms for DeepTech startups and cooperative societies, designed to meet founders where they are. He also emphasised the importance of incubators, market access, and cross-regional collaboration in helping ambitious founders scale from the Northeast to the nation and beyond.

Dr. Tej Chingtham, CEO, AIC-SMUTBI and Member, National Startup Advisory Council, delivered the welcome address, setting the tone for the Meet by reaffirming AIC-SMUTBI's commitment to nurturing early-stage innovation and technology-led entrepreneurship across the region.

Shri Ateesh Kumar Singh also met with the Mumbai Dabbawalas, who shared insights from their renowned logistics and delivery model during the event.

Ms. Diksha Rathore, Deputy Manager – Incubation and Entrepreneurship Development, represented BIRAC and accompanied the Hon'ble Chief Minister of Chhattisgarh Shri Vishnu Deo Sai during his visit to the newly inaugurated Subhash Chandra Bose Biotechnology Incubation Centre. The centre has been established through a joint collaboration between the Department of Biotechnology, Government of India, and the Department of Agriculture, Farmer Welfare & Biotechnology, Government of Chhattisgarh, with Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya (IGKV), Raipur, as the technical partner.

She also participated in three panel discussions across the conclave:
1. 𝗘𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗵𝗵𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗶𝘀𝗴𝗮𝗿𝗵 : highlighting biotechnology as an emerging sector for the state, built on its rich biodiversity, forest produce and agri-resources to help in creating impactful solutions that are the need of the hour
2. 𝗜𝗻𝗰𝘂𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗖𝗵𝗵𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗶𝘀𝗴𝗮𝗿𝗵 : outlining BIRAC's grant-in-aid and equity-based funding schemes that offer students, startups, industry, and academicians a de-risked, first-of-its-kind pathway from idea to enterprise. 
3. 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘂𝗲 : 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗵, 𝗜𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗖𝗵𝗵𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗶𝘀𝗴𝗮𝗿𝗵 : discussing the ways in which policy support and enabling ecosystems can empower young innovators across the state.

She emphasised the need to inculcate an entrepreneurial mindset among students as a key driver toward Viksit Bharat @2047, in the spirit of Make in India, Make for the World.

At the Valedictory Ceremony, Ms. Rathore joined Hon'ble Agriculture Minister of Chhattisgarh, Shri Ram Vichar Netam, for presentation of award cheques to the winners of the Startup Pitching session, product launch and the certificate distribution.

🌱C-CAMP, in collaboration with Ashraya Hastha Trust, has selected 11 innovations to drive climate action and sustainability in India and the world! #CCAMP #ClimateChange #Innovations #sustainability
 
These startups are working at the interface of climate change with healthcare, agriculture, and the environment, and represent the 1st cohort of the Centre of Excellence (CoE) for Sustainability & Climate Action at C-CAMP. 
 
The selected startups are —
 
* GenePath Diagnostics (climate x healthcare): a room-temperature stable open PCR platform for One Health detection of tropical vector-borne pathogens
* Prodancy Pvt Ltd (climate x healthcare): reusable peristaltic pulse lavage system
* AeroDel Technology Innovations Pvt Ltd (climate x healthcare): climate-responsive airway clearance & respiratory monitoring solutions for pollution and heat-stressed populations

* Intello Labs (climate x agri): AI-powered quality digitisation and digital market infrastructure for efficient fresh produce trade
* String Bio Private Limited (climate x agri): methane-derived growth stimulants for climate-resilient sugarcane production
* Tealaa Innovations (climate x agri): robotic sludge management system designed for aquaculture ponds

* Ossus Biorenewables (climate x environment): decarbonising industrial effluents using bio-electrochemical OB hydracel bioreactor and generating green hydrogen
* #BPC Bioproducts amylo(climate x environment): commercialising sustainable packaging with tailored biodegradable plastic solutions for India
* EarthKind Innovations Foods Biotech (climate x environment): programmable lipid platform using agricultural residue feedstocks
 * Intrinsic Foundries (climate x environment): microalgae-based point-source CO₂ capture & high-value biochemical biorefinery platform
* #BisketLabs (climate x environment): bio-based printed circuit board (PCB) substrates from agri-waste for circular electronics manufacturing

The CoE will offer these startups —
 🔸Funding support of up to INR 50 lakhs, 
 🔸Access to high-end incubation labs,

C-CAMP - supported, Udupi-based startup BlackFrog receives strong support from Hon’ble Minister Jyotiraditya M Scindia for taking life-saving vaccines to hard-to-reach locations in India’s North East, through its innovative cold-chain vaccine carrier technology.

In partnership with C-CAMP, Blackfrog has enabled the delivery of emergency vaccines and critical medical supplies — including insulin, blood products, breast milk and medical specimens — to some of the remotest locations in Assam and Manipur.

Its active cold-chain technology, Emvolio, maintains the required 2–8°C temperature range, preventing temperature-sensitive medicines and vaccines from degrading or losing their efficacy during last-mile transportation — helping ensure life-saving healthcare supplies reach even the hardest-to-reach communities safely and effectively

With C-CAMP’s support, the technology has also been deployed in remote locations across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

C-CAMP has also supported Blackfrog through multiple programmes, including IT BT Department, Karnataka #KSAPBIO50 cohort, Atal Innovation Mission Official #SeedFund cohort, and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) COVID Fund cohort; Blackfrog is also a #NBEC2019 winner.

Thank you, Hon'ble Minister, for your encouraging words!

In the social sector, outcome-based finance has a seductive promise. Pay only when impact happens. No results, no money. Pay for Success. (Unless you are the Intermediary.)

Who could argue with that? I don't. For the right problem. Where the intervention is proven, the delivery is commoditised and the outcome is measurable, outcome contracts make sense. The causal chain is known. The only open question is execution: will this operator/NGO deliver, at this price/scale? That is deterministic risk. It can be priced. It can be contracted.

Now take an idea from the lab to the last mile. Will the science hold outside the lab? Can it be manufactured at a target price? Will a smallholder farmer or a district hospital actually adopt it? Will it survive the system it enters? That is not execution risk. That is discovery risk. And discovery cannot be contracted in advance.

An instrument that pays only on predetermined outcomes will quietly favour work where the answer is already known. Applied to innovation, it doesn't de-risk anything. It selects against the risk worth taking.

Ask one question of any "impact bond" or "outcome-based" structure: if the intervention fails, whose money is lost? Too often, the honest answer is nobody's. The investors sit behind guarantees and first-loss cushions. The outcome payer is the same philanthropic pool that would have written a grant anyway. The outcomes were chosen because they were easy to count, not because they mattered. Goodhart would recognise the pattern.

And the intermediaries? They take their cut upfront. Structuring fees. Advisory fees. Evaluation fees. Platform fees. All paid whether the impact arrives or not. Pay for success, it turns out, applies to everyone except the people designing the deal. The only party with no skin in the game is the one selling skin in the game :)

Meanwhile, the real risk has not gone anywhere. It still sits with the implementing organisation and, ultimately, the community, the people least able to say no.
Risk capital for innovation has to be honest about what it is buying: probability, not certainty. That does not mean less accountability. It means a different unit of accountability.

Judge the portfolio, not each bet. Fund in stages, against learning milestones that advance or kill an idea. Publish kill rates. Report failures as data, not embarrassment. Be explicit about which risk each rupee underwrites, and who loses it if things go wrong.

Uncertainty is not an exemption from evidence. It is a reason to measure differently.

So here is a modest proposal for the outcome-finance industry. Put intermediary fees on the same terms as everyone else. Paid on success. Clawed back on failure. Watch how quickly the enthusiasm for complex structures cools.

Impact bonds price execution risk. Innovation is discovery risk. Confusing the two doesn't de-risk anything. It just moves the risk to those with the least power to refuse it, while the fees move the other way.

Single-Use doesn’t have to mean Only Use.  

What if something designed to be thrown away can come back as something useful?  

At PadCare Labs, used sanitary pads are being transformed using 5D recycling technology. The process recovers the pulp and plastic from sanitary waste, putting these materials back into productive use. Alongside collection and reverse logistics, this creates a circular system where the waste is treated as a resource rather than something to simply throw away. 

But sustainability is not only about materials. It is also about people. 

PadCare also creates a safer and more formal working environment for people in the waste management workforce, helping move workers away from unsafe landfills and towards workplaces with greater safety and access to benefits such as health and employee insurance.  

It is a reminder that sustainable innovation can create value in more than one place – in everyday products we use, in systems we build and for the people who keep them running. 

From sanitary waste today to diapers, tissue paper and textile waste tomorrow, PadCare is expanding what can be part of the circular economy. 

Curious to see how PadCare is making it happen?

B2B or B2C? Your customer decides how you should go to market. 👇

A strong product is only one part of the equation. Your Go-To-Market (GTM) strategy needs to change based on who you're selling to.

In B2B, buying decisions often involve multiple stakeholders, longer evaluation cycles, business value, reliability, and measurable results.

In B2C, the journey is often more direct, with factors such as price, convenience, brand, experience, and customer preference playing a major role.

For startups, understanding this difference can help you make better decisions around:

🔹 Who your real decision-maker is
🔹 What motivates your customer to buy
🔹 Where you should reach them
🔹 How your sales journey should work
🔹 Which metrics actually matter
